labels_to_ensure.description: A design problem to be worked through and written up

issues.title: Talk to Tracy Popp — tooling, output format, and the upstream handoff
issues.body:
Answer 1.2 revealed a whole processing step upstream of us that we did not know the shape of.

> Presently we have a person (Tracy Popp) who has responsibility to take content off these media formats as we receive them and "process" the content according to best practices of digital preservation (descriptive metadata, preservation metadata, administrative metadata, file format identification, etc.) and then puts it into a network drive space where the archivists are supposed to review and make final appraisal decisions. **This is our bottleneck.**

She also administers the Archives' software (answer 4.2), and BitCurator is in use (answer 4.1).

**She owns the step immediately upstream of ours. We have never spoken to her.**

### What to ask

- [ ] What does the preservation processing produce — which tool, what fields, what file format?
- [ ] Does that metadata travel with the content onto the network drive, or live separately?
- [ ] Which BitCurator components are actually in use?
- [ ] Is DROID running? Joanne was unsure (answer 4.1)
- [ ] Is there PII or sensitivity scanning already happening?
- [ ] Which of the 49 collections came from disk images vs file copies (answer 1.6 says some did)
- [ ] What is the network drive path, and what would read access involve?
- [ ] Total size on disk and file count of the 49
- [ ] Where does she see the handoff — what would make her job easier rather than more complex?

### Why it is a blocker

Stage 01 does format identification and produces technical metadata. **She may already be doing both.** Depending on the answer this either removes work from #53 or changes what it consumes. Building first and reconciling later is the expensive order.

Ask Joanne for the introduction on the follow-up call.

Schema placeholder: `s01_upstream_*` columns in v1.1, speculative until we see real output.

Reference: [archives-answers-2026-08.md](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/docs/archives-answers-2026-08.md)

issues.title: Get read access to the Archives network drive
issues.body:
**Replaces the physical-drive access ask, which was solving the wrong problem.**

Answer 1.2: material is already off the media and on an Archives network drive, preservation-processed. Answer 1.4: 49 collections are sitting there now.

So we do not need a machine with a USB port and someone to plug drives in. **We need read permission on a network share** — a permissions conversation rather than a logistics one, and a much smaller ask.

Joanne offered in answer 1.3 to talk to Tracy and IT about finding a machine for connecting media. **Re-scope that before she spends capital on it** — ask for share access instead.

- [ ] Identify the share and its path
- [ ] Establish who grants read access
- [ ] Confirm read-only is acceptable to them and sufficient for us
- [ ] Confirm whether it is reachable from the processing host or needs VPN
- [ ] Run a directory listing — this closes the last open item from question 1.7
- [ ] `du -sh` for total size

Once this lands, several things unblock at once: the directory listing, the size figure, and the first inventory on material that is not a Box extract.

**Working-copy location is a separate open question.** Answer 5.6: "I will find out." That holds full unreviewed accession contents including unreviewed personal information, so it needs its own location, access control and clearing rule. Chase on the call.

issues.title: Draft the appraisal ruleset from Joanne's guidance and send it back for confirmation
issues.body:
Answers 3.2 and 3.3 give the first written appraisal guidance we have. It is not a policy, but it is enough to draft rules from — which turns the ask in #40 from "write us a policy" into "check whether we read yours correctly." Much easier to say yes to.

- [ ] Two rulesets, `personal_papers` and `administrative` — they differ substantively
- [ ] Retain rules from answer 3.2, discard rules from answer 3.3
- [ ] Discipline-conditional handling of drafts, selected by `profile_field` (answer 3.2: valuable for humanities scholars, discardable for others)
- [ ] Sensitivity precedence encoded — HR and personnel material never auto-discards
- [ ] Each rule named, so `s02_rule_matched` says which one fired
- [ ] Written up in plain language and sent to Joanne and Bethany for confirmation
- [ ] Run against the 50-file sample from #40 to check our reading against theirs

Lands in `src/schema/rules/{personal_papers,administrative}.py`.

**The thing to flag when sending it back:** Joanne listed HR material as both routinely discardable and sensitive. We have treated those as different dispositions — sensitive material routes to a supervising archivist rather than to discard, always. That is a change we made on her behalf and she should get the chance to disagree with it.

issues.title: Design decision: how item-level description attaches to a folder-level finding aid
issues.body:
Joanne asked the sharper version of our own question back at us (answer 5.8):

> Are you imagining a finding aid that provides item-level details, and that the build will be able to somehow automatically update existing finding aids? Most of the work in the Archives doesn't go to item level in the finding aids. However, the Sousa Archives and Center for American Music does. Perhaps we can find a way to incorporate item-level info about digital accessions into an existing folder-level-only finding aid?

The problem: we generate description per file. The Archives describes at collection and folder level. **Pushing thousands of item records into a folder-level finding aid would swamp it and make it worse, not better.**

**Likely shape**, from Joanne's email about ArchivesSpace: description lives in our own store, and the finding aid gains a **link** at folder level rather than item records being pushed into it. That matches how she describes wanting it to work — links in ArchivesSpace out to files stored in Medusa or the Digital Library.

- [ ] Study the Sousa item-level finding aid as the model: https://archon.library.illinois.edu/archives/index.php?p=collections/controlcard&id=3132&q=sousa
- [ ] Establish what ArchivesSpace can accept and link to
- [ ] Propose the attachment model to Joanne with a worked example
- [ ] Decision recorded here with reasoning

Shapes what #66 produces. Worth resolving before building the crosswalk.

The Sousa finding aid is the first concrete example of "good" we have been given — build toward it rather than toward a specification.

issues.title: Design decision: repository-neutral export with a per-destination adapter
issues.body:
Answer 5.4 carries a risk worth designing around:

> ...we are just about to embark upon a "digital strategies" exercise to clarify all the various ways the Library (and Archives) need and use digital systems and content. Part of that is to also be looking at a **replacement for Medusa — likely going to a commercial product.**

**Building tightly to Medusa's ingest format is building to something with a known expiry.**

Proposal: the pipeline emits a **repository-neutral package**, and a thin adapter maps it to whatever the destination currently is.

```
src/delivery/
  package.py              repository-neutral output
  adapters/medusa.py
  adapters/digital_library.py
  adapters/archivesspace.py
```

Costs little now. Saves a rebuild when Medusa is replaced.

- [ ] Define the neutral package format
- [ ] Adapter interface spec
- [ ] Medusa adapter, once we know what it expects (answer 5.5: Joanne is finding out who to ask)
- [ ] Decision recorded here

**Also worth asking:** whether we can be represented in the digital strategies exercise. A system that appraises and describes born-digital accessions at scale is squarely within its scope, and being downstream of that conversation rather than inside it is how you end up retrofitting.

issues.title: Retention clock and disposal workflow
issues.body:
Answer 5.7 corrected a design position I had over-applied, and Joanne is right:

> Which software never deletes? Regardless, once we have COMPLETED the selection stage of accessioning, everything else should be deleted. If there is a chance we need more time to decide on selection decisions, we will want a clear time period for when that content needs to be acted on. **This has been one of our challenges as we didn't set such a time period when the backlog content we have was originally brought in.**

We had been saying "the software never deletes" as a safety property. That is true of the *software's autonomous behaviour*, but I had let it become a description of the archival lifecycle, which it is not. The Archives disposes of material deliberately after selection, and answer 6.4 confirms nothing externally prevents it.

**The last sentence is the important one.** The absence of a retention clock is what created the backlog. Building one in addresses the cause, not the symptom.

### Design

- The pipeline **never deletes autonomously** — unchanged, non-negotiable
- It **does** provide a deletion action: batched, approved by the accession archivist (answer 6.5), recorded with who and when
- Clock starts at `selection_completed_at`, not at ingest — material under active consideration is never on a timer
- **`restricted_review` material is never auto-proposed for disposal**
- **The manifest row survives deletion of the content** — path, hash, size, dates, decision and rationale all retained. That is the audit trail, it is tiny, and destroying it would make the disposal unaccountable

Schema v1.1: `dp_eligible_at`, `dp_proposed_at`, `dp_approved_by`, `dp_approved_at`, `dp_batch_id`, `dp_executed_at`, `dp_manifest_retained`.

- [ ] **Ask Joanne what retention window she wants.** Schema defaults to 180 days; she asked for "a clear time period" without naming one
- [ ] Build the batch approval flow into the review queue (#68)
- [ ] Answer her question directly on the call — she deserves a straight response, not a restatement of the design

Answer 6.4 for the record: no schedule requires disposal. Disposition follows the appraisal decision and the Deed of Gift terms where one exists.

issues.title: Accession profile template, and one real profile to test it
issues.body:
Answer 3.1, confirmed:

> Yes, it is possible to put together short profiles. In fact, in most cases we shouldn't be acquiring content from anonymous people so having some sort of "bio" info on them makes perfect sense.

**This is more valuable than it looks.** It is not just context to hand a model — per answer 3.2, whether drafts are worth keeping depends on the person's discipline. So `profile_field` is a **rule selector**: a branch in the code, not a hint in a prompt.

- [ ] Template rather than free text — five fields, half a page: person, department, field/discipline, active years, what they worked on
- [ ] One real profile for one real accession, to test the format against something actual
- [ ] Wire `profile_field` into ruleset selection
- [ ] Confirm the field vocabulary is coarse enough to be reliable (humanities / sciences / social sciences / administrative is probably enough)

Schema v1.1: the `profile_*` block on `accessions.parquet`.

Ask for one profile, not 49. The format has to survive contact with a real person first.

issues.title: Confidentiality agreement template for the Archives
issues.body:
Joanne asked us a question and it deserves a real answer rather than a shrug. Answer 7.5:

> I would like both Gauri and you to have permissions to see unredacted content during processing. **Is there any sort of template for an NDA that AITS has everyone sign we can model here in the Archives?** Presently, we are not very tight about that sort of control.

She is asking us to help formalise something the Archives currently does informally. Reasonable ask, cheap goodwill, and it makes the access question in #43 easier to answer.

- [ ] Find out what AITS uses for confidentiality agreements
- [ ] Ask Brent — he will know the RIMS-side answer
- [ ] Send Joanne whatever exists, or say plainly if nothing does

Not blocking anything. Small, and worth doing promptly because she asked.
